On Thu, 30 Nov 2000 sprice at usgs.gov wrote:

> Hi,
> 
>      Since S-Plus is so great for data manipulation,  I want to pose this
> question with regard to data output.  As a simple example, if I have a
> dataframe (5 x 3) with the fields: ID, X1, Y1, X2, Y2  and I want to create

> below (for the ESRI tribe - yes, I'm creating a generate file).  Is there a
> way to do this in S-Plus or am I left with outputting a regular ASCII file
> and then using awk/sed?  Any suggestions would be welcomed.  Thanks.

df <- data.frame(ID=1:3, X1=c(3,5,7), Y1=c(3,5,7), X2=c(4,6,8),Y2=c(4,6,8))
attach(df)
out <- paste(ID, "\n", X1, ",", Y1, "\n", X2, ",", Y2, "\nEND", sep="")

# as required.

product of an arbitrary column with itself.  Specify more clearly

messages.subject_clean: Rounding timeDate or timeSeries to nearest time unit
messages.body_plain:
Working with
Version 5.1 Release 1 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.5 : 1999

I have a timeSeries object where the data were collected once per 
minute, with the time recorded to the nearest second. I'd like to 
round them to the nearest minute.

The align() function works, unless there are gaps, as in the example 
below. Then it fills in the gaps.

>  foom
         Positions 1
 12-01-00 10:30:27 9
 12-01-00 10:31:27 6
 12-01-00 10:32:27 6
 12-01-00 10:40:27 5
 12-01-00 10:41:27 7
 12-01-00 10:42:27 7

>  align(foom,by='minutes',how='nearest')
         Positions 1
 12-01-00 10:30:00 9
 12-01-00 10:31:00 6
 12-01-00 10:32:00 6
 12-01-00 10:33:00 6
 12-01-00 10:34:00 6
 12-01-00 10:35:00 6
 12-01-00 10:36:00 6
 12-01-00 10:37:00 5
 12-01-00 10:38:00 5
 12-01-00 10:39:00 5
 12-01-00 10:40:00 5
 12-01-00 10:41:00 7
 12-01-00 10:42:00 7
 12-01-00 10:43:00 7
>
[align() also adds data to the end! Unless you specify error.how='drop')]

I can think of two ways to do it that are "ugly." One is to convert 
the positions to character strings using a format that omits the 
seconds, then convert back to timeDate class with the same format. 
The other is to convert to numeric, transform days to to minutes, 
round, and convert back to timeDate.

I'd appreciate suggestions for better ways, or pointers to built-in 
functions I should have found but didn't.

Thanks
-Don

p.s.
Additional comments.

More generally, I can envisage, for example, data collected once per 
hour, recorded to the nearest minute and second, and wanting to round 
up or down to the nearest hour. Or rounding time-date data to any 
desired time interval. Analogous to round(), ceiling() and floor() 
for numeric data. align() would do it, except for the gaps. align() 
also will fail grossly for data that is out of time order, which can 
easily happen with timeDate data.

round() doesn't work:
>  round(positions(foom))
Problem in round(positions(foom)): Function does not make sense for times

Conceptually, however, it does make sense; it just needs a 'by' 
argument to specify what time interval to round to. More generally, 
these functions should operate on objects of class timeDate, rather 
than or in addition to timeSeries objects.

One could use the mdy() and hms() functions to get the job done in 
several steps.

>  mdy(positions(foom))
  month day year
1    12   1 2000
2    12   1 2000
3    12   1 2000
4    12   1 2000
5    12   1 2000
6    12   1 2000
>  hms(positions(foom))
  hour minute second ms
1   10     30     27  0
2   10     31     27  0
3   10     32     27  0
4   10     40     27  0
5   10     41     27  0
6   10     42     27  0
--
--------------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Department
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Livermore, CA, USA
--------------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
Richard E Hoskins asks the seminal question:

> 
> If the following works ...
> 
> wtgms.f2[wtgms.f2 < 1000]
>  [1] 765  NA  NA 635  NA  NA  NA 850 590  NA  NA 992 840  NA 713 539
> [17] 964 595 856 540 595 975 580 840 544  NA 652 650 539 693 340 539
> [33]  NA  NA  NA 560  NA  NA  NA 879 700 794  NA  NA  NA
> 
> Why doesn't the following?
> 
> wtgms.f2[wtgms.f2 != NA]  (I want to get all non-missing elements in
> wtgms.f2)
>    [1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA
>   [21] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA

This is a good opportunity to get your model on how NA works within S
straight.  The first thing to settle completely in your mind is that "NA" is
not a value, it is a marker for something that is NOT there.  This is the
case whether it appears in data or in expressions.

In this light consider the expression "wtgms.f2 != NA".  The right hand side
of the inequality is not supplied, it is only marked as being NOT AVAILABLE.
Hence the expression itself cannot (yet) be evaluated.  Hence all values
that might have depended on it are likewise NOT AVAILABLE.  Hence the
behaviour you see.

In many systems the counterpart of NA is simply another value, but one that
will never legitimately be used as data, even though it can be used in
expressions, so your question is not entirely surprising.  

The exact position with NA is, of course, a little more complex than this as
it often covers three sorts of, let's say, "ineffable" values, namely true
NAs, NaNs and Infs, but that's another story....

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: RE: [Int_snews] Re: Unique for matrices
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have two minor problems with Bill's table.rows() function below.  First,
it doesn't work on data.frames (at least not under Splus 4.5 for windows),
because object tab is a 1D array, and cbind.data.frame will not treat it as
a column.  Since the question was about matrices, this is a reasonable
limitation.  But a simple change would allow data.frames to work also.

Second, when dum is a matrix, dum.strings shows up as row names of the
output.  This is mostly an aesthetic quibble, though for big matrices its
rather wasteful of memory too.

Phil Spector some years ago contributed to this list a function,
table.mat(), to solve this problem.  I have since modified Phil's function
in a variety of ways, not least of which is to add the sort of reliability
that Bill suggests below (using sep = "\001" in paste, and making sure that
paste does not mistakenly interpret column names as argument names).  The
function works for a matrix, a vector, or a data.frame, including a
data.frame that contains a matrix as a list component.

Cheers,
Scott

================================
Scott D. Chasalow
Cereon Genomics

Email: Scott.Chasalow at cereon.com
================================ 

=========================================================================
"table.mat"<-
function(mat, order.rows = T, sep = "\001")
{
#  DATE INSTALLED:  30 Nov 1993             LAST REVISED:  04 Dec 2000 
#  AUTHOR:  Phil Spector  (spector at stat.berkeley.edu)
#  REVISED BY: Scott D. Chasalow (Scott.Chasalow at cereon.com)
#
#  DESCRIPTION:
#        Counts occurrences of rows in a data.frame or matrix.
#
#  ARGUMENTS:  
#  mat:  a matrix, data frame, or vector
#  order.rows:  a logical value.  If true,  rows of result are sorted.
#  sep:  a character string to use as separator when pasting together
#        columns of mat.  Thus the value must not be present in mat.
#        The default is "\001" (control-A).
#
#  VALUE:
#        A data frame with a column for each column in data.frame(mat), 
#        and a final column of counts appended; rows are the UNIQUE rows
#        of mat.  A similar result, but as a multi-way array,  may be
#        obtained with the call, do.call("table", as.data.frame(mat)).
#
#  SEE ALSO:
#        match.mat, unique.mat
#
     nms <- NULL
     if(!is.data.frame(mat)) {
          nms <- dimnames(mat)[[2]]
          mat <- as.data.frame(mat)
     }
     if(any(sapply(mat, is.matrix))) {
          mat <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(mat), optional = T)
          if(!is.null(nms))
               names(mat) <- nms
     }
     mat.list <- as.list(mat)
     names(mat.list) <- NULL     # In case any names are args to paste
     pmat <- do.call("paste", c(list(sep = sep), mat.list))
     which <- !duplicated(pmat)
     mat.use <- mat[which,  , drop = F]
     uniq.pmat <- pmat[which]
     mat.tab <- table(factor(pmat, levels = uniq.pmat))
     cnt <- mat.tab[match(uniq.pmat, names(mat.tab))]
     names(cnt) <- NULL     # So these names are not part of output
     mat.use$Count <- cnt
     if(order.rows) {
          tmp <- as.list(mat.use)
          names(tmp) <- NULL     # In case any names are args to order
          mat.use <- mat.use[do.call("order", tmp),  ]
     }
     row.names(mat.use) <- as.character(1:dim(mat.use)[1])
     mat.use
}
=====================================================================

-----Original Message-----
From: Bill Dunlap [mailto:bill at statsci.com]
Sent: Tuesday, 28 November, 2000 16:28
To: Anne York
Cc: Phil Corbett; S News
Subject: Re: [Int_snews] Re: [S] Unique for matrices

On Tue, 28 Nov 2000, Anne York wrote:

> Here is one  method:
> Suppose your matrix is called dum:
> 1. convert the matrix into a vector of strings:
> dum.strings_apply(dum,1,paste,collapse="")

This is about what I'd recommend, but 2 changes can make it
more reliable and faster.

(reliability) I like to use "\001" as the separator so that it doesn't
        confound, e.g., 12 3 and 1 23.  (This assumes that "\001",
control-A,
        doesn't show up in data often).

(speed) Paste the columns together in one call to paste instead
        of calling paste on each row.  E.g.,
                dum.list <- as.list(data.frame(dum))
                names(dum.list)<-NULL
                dum.strings <- do.call("paste", c(list(sep="\001"),
dum.list))
        (We take off the names of the data frame so paste() doesn't
        interpret them as argument names).

The complete function would be

unique.rows1 <- function(dum) {
        dum.list <- as.list(data.frame(dum))
        names(dum.list) <- NULL
        dum.strings <- do.call("paste", c(list(sep = "\001"), dum.list))
        dum[match(unique(dum.strings), dum.strings),  ]
}

You can add a column of counts with the following function

table.rows <- function(dum) {
        dum.list <- as.list(data.frame(dum))
        names(dum.list) <- NULL
        dum.strings <- do.call("paste", c(list(sep = "\001"), dum.list))
        tab <- table(factor(dum.strings, levels = unique(dum.strings)))
        cbind(dum[match(unique(dum.strings), dum.strings),  ], count = tab)
}

> I am trying to estimate cumulants of a sample distribution 
> which is expected to be slightly non-normal (say, 
> t-distribution with ~15 degrees of freedom, or 
> chi-square with ~20 df).  I am using standard analytical 
> expressions of cumulants through moments. The latter, as far 
> as I know are assumed to be unbiased. I have only 
> comparatively small sample, about, say,
> 40 to 100 datapoints. I was completely shocked how biased are 
> the sample cumulants! 

Why?  The standard analytical expressions are non-linear functions of
quantities that themselves are known to be biased estimators of their
population counterparts.  While unbiasedness might be considered possible, I
would hardly rate it as likely.

In fact this problem has a long and illustrious history.  R A Fisher posed,
and solved the following problem: "Find a homogeneous polynomial function of
the sample of degree r that is an unbiased estimator of the rth cumulant of
the distribution".  The solution came to be knows as the k-statistics of the
sample.  They start off with the sample mean and the usual sample variance
(with the n-1 divisor).  Kendall and Stuart vol.1, for example, somewhat
exuberantly present the first 9 or 10, as I recall, though I can't really
imagine why.

The extension to multivariate distributions was (I think) tackled by Tukey
and his "polykays" are the result, I seem to recall.

> I am not saying here about their 
> variances which are naturally expected to be large. Does 
> anybody of you guys know any unbiased approach to estimating 
> sample cumulants?

Yes, use k-statistics.  I have always found this a fairly artificial
problem, though.  How often does one really get a homogeneous sample?  How
often does one really get one large enough to make estimation of the higher
order cumulants a realistic thing to do?  What do you do with them when you
get them?

It is conceivably possible you might want to use, say, k3 and k4 in

convinced otherwise, though.  Life is a long learning process.)

messages.body_plain:
Here is the long-awaited (by some of you, anyway) summary to my question
on copying column names. Here is my original question:
S-PLUS 2000 Windows 2000
I would like to copy specific columns (not all) from one data frame into
another, data and column names altogether. The problem is in copying
the column names. I am able to copy all the column names from one data
frame to another using names(), but names() and name.cols() have not
been able to copy only specific column names for me, particularly if I
just want to copy one column name or if I want to copy columns that are
not sequential. There must be a function or command or combination of
commands that will copy the column names along with the data of columns
that I specify.
For example, I have a logical vector named 'good' that specifies which
columns in a data frame meet certain specifications. I want to copy
those columns with their names and data into another data frame that may
already have data in it, or not. Any ideas?

Yes, there were ideas. The first one is from BERT GUNTER:
If I understand you correctly, just use cbind as in (where df1 and df2
are
data frames or matrices):
df2_cbind(df1[,c(2,4,7,10,11)],df2)
This will put the copied columns at the beginning; the other way round
does
them at the end.
Of course, the number of rows must be the same in both dataframes or it
won't work.

Here's an interesting strategy from PETER ALSPACH:
os> win.new
one two three a b e 
1 1 2 3 11 12 15
2 1 2 3 11 12 15
3 1 2 3 11 12 15
4 1 2 3 11 12 15
os> win.test
one two three 
1 1 2 3
2 1 2 3
3 1 2 3
4 1 2 3
os> win.add
a b c d e 
1 11 12 13 14 15
2 11 12 13 14 15
3 11 12 13 14 15
4 11 12 13 14 15
os> good
[1] T T F F T
os> win.new <- cbind(win.test, win.add[,good])
os> win.new
one two three a b e 
1 1 2 3 11 12 15
2 1 2 3 11 12 15
3 1 2 3 11 12 15
4 1 2 3 11 12 15
os> 
BUT
os> win.new <- cbind(win.test[,1:2], win.add[,good], win.test[,3])
os> win.new
one two a b e X3 
1 1 2 11 12 15 3
2 1 2 11 12 15 3
3 1 2 11 12 15 3
4 1 2 11 12 15 3
os> names(win.new) <- c(names(win.test[1:2]), names(win.add)[good], 
names(win.test[3]))
os> win.new
one two a b e three 
1 1 2 11 12 15 3
2 1 2 11 12 15 3
3 1 2 11 12 15 3
4 1 2 11 12 15 3

The following is from PATRICK CONNOLLY:
Unless your data has odd things I'm not thinking of, if x is your
dataframe with data you wish to move to dataframe y, you could do
this:
y[, names(x)[good]] <- x[, good]
I assume you'll be taking the precautions necessary to deal with
similar named columns being overwritten. The process might get tricky
if there is only one TRUE in good. Your y dataframe needs to exist. It's
a
safe guess that the first column of two will be identical to a couple
of columns of x, let's say, e.g.
y <- x[, c(3,1)]
Then it should work fine.

Simply stated by NICK ELLIS:
new.df <- cbind(new.df,old.df[good])
or
new.df <- cbind(new.df,old.df[,good])

This is from RENAUD LANCELOT:
Suppose your original dataset is called Data, and the final one is
called New:
New <- Data[ , names(Data)[good]]
should do what you want.

Here is one from ROGER NGOUENET:
If you are using command line, maybe the following can help.
> testdf <- data.frame(a=1:5,b=6:10,c=1:5)
> testdf
a b c 
1 1 6 1
2 2 7 2
3 3 8 3
4 4 9 4
5 5 10 5
> testdf[,c(T,F,T)]
a c 
1 1 1
2 2 2
3 3 3
4 4 4
5 5 5
> data2 <- matrix(rnorm(20), 5)
> data2
[,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] 
[1,] 0.20543264 -1.0032371 0.1171264 -0.8269112
[2,] 1.09449833 0.6050628 0.3061682 -0.2363855
[3,] 0.01580222 1.7070940 -1.5148787 -0.3806734
[4,] -2.03799218 1.9848074 -0.5567222 -0.7257833
[5,] 0.35748014 -1.0054270 1.0196144 0.1769254
> cbind(testdf, data2)
a b c 1 2 3 4 
1 1 6 1 0.20543264 -1.0032371 0.1171264 -0.8269112
2 2 7 2 1.09449833 0.6050628 0.3061682 -0.2363855
3 3 8 3 0.01580222 1.7070940 -1.5148787 -0.3806734
4 4 9 4 -2.03799218 1.9848074 -0.5567222 -0.7257833
5 5 10 5 0.35748014 -1.0054270 1.0196144 0.1769254
> cbind(testdf[,c(T,F,T)], data2[,-1])
a c 1 2 3 
1 1 1 -1.0032371 0.1171264 -0.8269112
2 2 2 0.6050628 0.3061682 -0.2363855
3 3 3 1.7070940 -1.5148787 -0.3806734
4 4 4 1.9848074 -0.5567222 -0.7257833
5 5 5 -1.0054270 1.0196144 0.1769254
(NOTE from Winnie: I am using a script)

Finally, from our local expert CHUCK TAYLOR at MathSoft:
Use copy.col(). Args are
> args(copy.col.default) 
function(target, target.start.col, source, source.col.spec, overwrite =
F)

It seems like cbind() is the common link here, although copy.col() looks
like a good possibility, too. Since I've been fighting my computer over
the last week, I haven't come to a final conclusion about which one I
will use, but I really appreciate the inputs and will save them for
future reference.

messages.subject: SUM: "really" formatted ASCII export
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Many thanks to all who responded - there were a total of 9 replies.  There
are several way to get the desired ASCII file format from the data frame,
which attests to the strength of S-PLUS in data manipulation. Following are
the original test data and responses with authors (in order received).

Data Frame
ID X1 Y1 X2 Y2
1   3    3   4     4
2   5    5   6     6
3   7    7   8     8

Desired Output Ascii File Format
1
3,3
4,4
END
2
5,5
6,6
END
3
7,7
8,8
END
END

******************** Peter Alspach ***************
One way - and there are doubtless others:

> susan <- read.table('clipboard', header=T)
> susan
  ID X1 Y1 X2 Y2
1  1  3  3  4  4
2  2  5  5  6  6
3  3  7  7  8  8
> sue <- cbind(susan[,1], paste(susan[,2], susan[,3], sep=','), paste(susan
[,4], susan[,5], sep=','), rep('END', dim(susan)[1]))
> sue
     [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
[1,] "1"  "3,3" "4,4" "END"
[2,] "2"  "5,5" "6,6" "END"
[3,] "3"  "7,7" "8,8" "END"
> as.vector(t(sue))
 [1] "1"   "3,3" "4,4" "END" "2"   "5,5" "6,6" "END" "3"
[10] "7,7" "8,8" "END"

Hence you could output as.vector(t(sue))

******************************************************

*************** Bill Dunlap ************************
The following seems to do what you want without taking too much time
or code.  For really large datasets you may need to do the output in
several chunks (say 100,000 rows at a time) to save memory.

f <- function(d, file)
{
        tmp <- paste(sep = "", d$ID, "\n", d$X1, ",", d$Y1, "\n", d$X2,
",",
                d$Y2, "\nEND")
        cat(tmp, "END", sep = "\n", file = file)
}

******************************************************

************* Bill Venables ***********************

m <- data.frame(ID=1:10, x1=1:10, y1=10:1, x2=11:10, y2=20:11)
attach(m)
ahem <- paste(ID, paste(x1, y1, sep=","),
                  paste(x2, y2, sep=","),
                  "END\n", sep="\n")
sink("ASCII.txt")
cat(ahem)
cat("END\n")

********************************************************

************ Nick Ellis *******************************

Simply put cat inside a loop, thus:

> for (i in 1:nrow(dat)){
     d<-dat[i,]
     cat(d$ID,"\n")
     cat(d$X1,",",d$Y1,"\n",sep="")
     cat(d$X2,",",d$Y2,"\n",sep="")
     cat("END\n")
}
1
3,3
4,4
END
2
5,5
6,6
END
3
7,7
8,8
END

To get it in a file, use sink(....). Empty sink() sends output back to
terminal.

> sink("output.dat")
> for (i in 1:nrow(dat)){
     d<-dat[i,]
     cat(d$ID,"\n")
     cat(d$X1,",",d$Y1,"\n",sep="")
     cat(d$X2,",",d$Y2,"\n",sep="")
     cat("END\n")
}
> sink()

***********************************************************

*******  Patrick Connolly *******************************

If your dataframe is called x, this function will give what you need.
Depending on what system you use, it is simple to get it from standard
output to a file.

function()
{
    for(i in seq(nrow(x))) {
       cat(paste(i))
       cat("\n")
       cat(paste(x[i, c("X1", "Y1")], collapse = ","))
       cat("\n")
       cat(paste(x[i, c("X2", "Y2")], collapse = ","))
       cat("\nEND\n")
    }
    cat("END\n")
}

*********************************************************

***** Charles C. Berry ********************************

I think you need 'cat'

e.g.

> cat(t(expand.grid(1:2,3:4,5:6)),"END\n",sep=c("\n",",","\nEND\n"))
1
3,5
END
2
3,5
END
[snip]

I don't quite follow the formatting, but if you check the help for
'cat' you'll see that 'sep' can use a vector. If you are familiar with
'rep', this too should help.

*******************************************************

******************* Henrik Aalborg Nielsen ******

Here is one solution:

If 'df' is your data frame, then create a new one with some cols. pasted
together:

df2 <- data.frame(ID = df$ID, x1y1 = paste(df$x1, df$y1, sep = ","),
                  x2y2 = paste(df$x2, df$y2, sep = ","))

And then write the file as:

write.table(df2, sep="\n", end="\nEND\n", dim=F, file="test.dat")
write.table(rep("END",2), append=T, file="test.dat")

*******************************************************

********************* Prof Brian D. Ripley *********
cat() is the tool here.  A vectorised solution is

df <- data.frame(ID=1:3, X1=c(3,5,7), Y1=c(3,5,7), X2=c(4,6,8),Y2=c(4,6,8))
attach(df)
out <- paste(ID, "\n", X1, ",", Y1, "\n", X2, ",", Y2, "\nEND", sep="")
detach()
cat(out, file="outfile", sep="\n")

# as required.

[ example omitted, reproduced by above lines ]

********************************************************

********************* Doug Mciver  ******************

I?just saw your question on the Splus mailing list.? This isn't the most
elegant solution but it works.? For longer matricies you can replace the c
() functions with rep().

I?personally think that the awk/sed or perl solutions are probably better
but here is one way to do this in S.

Doug

tmp
???? [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
[1,]??? 1??? 3??? 3??? 4??? 4
[2,]??? 2??? 5??? 5??? 6??? 6
[3,]??? 3??? 7??? 7??? 8??? 8

for(i in c(2,4)){ tmp2 <- cbind(tmp2,c(paste(as.character(tmp
[,i]),",")),tmp[,i+1])}

[1,] "1"? ""?? "3"? "3"? "4"? "4"? "END" ""
[2,] "2"? ""?? "5"? "5"? "6"? "6"? "END" ""
[3,] "3"? ""?? "7"? "7"? "8"? "8"? "END" ""
write(file = "tmp", ncol = 2, t(tmp2))

messages.subject: Annoying bug-let in predict.glm()?
messages.body_plain:
Hi. Here's something that's bothered me for a while. Right now I'm on S-Plus
2000, release 3, under NT.

Consider building a simple glm model for the Kyphosis response in the
kyphosis (built-in) data set:

> kyph.glm <- glm (Kyphosis ~ ., data = kyphosis, family=binomial)

So far, so good: Now suppose I want to do some prediction:

> predict (kyph.glm, kyphosis[1:2,], type = "response")
         1        2 
 0.2570008 0.122469
Warning messages:
  Variable Kyphosis is not a factor in: model.frame.default(terms.object,
data, xlevels = xlevels)

This is annoying. Kyphosis *is* a factor, and furthermore, I don't care,
because I'm not using that column for prediction.

> predict (kyph.glm, type = "response")[1:2] # This works okay...

> new.data <- kyphosis[1:2,2:4]         # Remove "Kyphosis" column
> predict (kyph.glm, new.data, type = "response") # This still doesn't work
         1        2 
 0.2570008 0.122469
Warning messages:
  Variable Kyphosis is not a factor in: model.frame.default(terms.object,
data, xlevels = xlevels)
>

The problem is, as the message suggests, in model.frame.default, or at least
that's where the message is being generated. Can anyone explain to me what's
going on?

Thanks,
Sam Buttrey

messages.subject: While we are talking about predict.glm
messages.subject_clean: While we are talking about predict.glm
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

While we are on the subject of predict.glm here is another behaviour that I
have a hard time to cope with.  When subsetting a data set on a factor variable
with more that two levels and using that variable, with the remaining levels, in
the model glm will drop the unused level(s), which is as expected, but
predict.glm can't cope with this, complaining about a new level in that
variable, even if the level is unusued in the new data frame.
I know that predict.gam can be used in such
cases but when the modeling and validation data sets have well over 300K
observations I find that using predict.gam is a big waste of time.  I used the
builtin kyphosis data frame to illustrate my point.

First create a new factor in kyphosis.

> ttt.kyph <- cbind(kyphosis, Num.fact = cut(kyphosis$Number,
+                               breaks = c(2, 3, 4, 5, Inf),
+                               labels = c('first', 'second', 'third', 
'fourth'),
+                               include.lowest = T))

Now split the new data frame in modeling and validation samples.

> ttt.index <- sample(1:dim(ttt.kyph)[1], 40, replace = F)
> ttt.sample <- ttt.kyph[ttt.index, ]
> ttt.valid <- ttt.kyph[-ttt.index, ]

Check that all levels of the new factor are represented in both samples.

> frequence(ttt.sample$Num.fact)
       Frequency Percent Cum.Freq Cum.Percent
 first        17    42.5       17        42.5
second         9    22.5       26        65.0
 third         8    20.0       34        85.0
fourth         6    15.0       40       100.0

> frequence(ttt.valid$Num.fact)
       Frequency Percent Cum.Freq Cum.Percent
 first        18   43.90       18       43.90
second         9   21.95       27       65.85
 third         9   21.95       36       87.80
fourth         5   12.20       41      100.00

The model, on a subset of the sample data frame, for sake of argument we subset
on the first level, but since Num.fact has four levels the variable can still
be used in a model.

> ttt.glm <- glm(Kyphosis ~ Age + Start + Num.fact, family = binomial,
+                data = ttt.sample,
+                subset = ttt.sample$Num.fact != levels(ttt.sample$Num.fact)[1])

Check that the first level was dropped.

> coef(summary(ttt.glm))
                     Value Std. Error    t value
   (Intercept) -74.0216451  80.917862 -0.9147751
           Age   0.9387336   1.006537  0.9326373
         Start  -8.0022783   8.591708 -0.9313955
 Num.factthird  31.7065000  40.260110  0.7875413
Num.factfourth  93.9967082 200.485497  0.4688454

Indeed it was.

Now use predict.glm on the validation data set excluding the first level of 
Num.fact.

> predict(ttt.glm, newdata = ttt.valid[ttt.valid$Num.fact !=
+                    levels(ttt.valid$Num.fact)[1], ], type = 'response')

Error in model.frame.default(terms.object, data, x..: factor Num.fact has new le
vel(s) first

Confirm that the first level has 0 frequency.

> frequence(ttt.valid[ttt.valid$Num.fact !=
+                    levels(ttt.valid$Num.fact)[1], 'Num.fact'])

       Frequency Percent Cum.Freq Cum.Percent
 first         0    0.00        0        0.00
second         9   39.13        9       39.13
 third         9   39.13       18       78.26
fourth         5   21.74       23      100.00

Of course predict.gam can handle that.

> predict.gam(ttt.glm, newdata = ttt.valid[ttt.valid$Num.fact !=
+                    levels(ttt.valid$Num.fact)[1], ], type = 'response')

             5            10            11            14            18 19
 2.220446e-016 1.057888e-009 2.220446e-016 2.220446e-016 2.210312e-012  1
            21            27        37            40            42 43 45
 2.220446e-016 2.220446e-016 0.7469675 2.220446e-016 2.220446e-016  1  1
            58         61 64            67            68            72
 2.220446e-016 0.01521673  1 2.220446e-016 2.220446e-016 2.220446e-016
            74 76            78            83
 2.220446e-016  1 1.953828e-012 2.220446e-016

I find this behaviour of predict.glm very annoying, why can't it detect, from
the input model, that one of the levels of Num.fact was not used?

Thanks,

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat

messages.body_plain:
Dear Everybody,

Version 0.5 of the smart prediction library smartpred is now
available.

The smartpred library consists of some modified existing and new
functions to fix a problem relating to the modelling functions lm and
glm. The modified versions now remember the "parameters" of special
smartened functions (bs, ns, scale and poly are supplied). We call this
"smart" prediction. The parameters are saved on the fitted model
object, and are retrieved when predictions are made from the model.
Users can easily smarten their own functions - guidelines are given.
Another problem (or better, inconvenient convention) of lm not handling
factors conveniently is also rectified in some older versions of
S-PLUS (3.x, 5.x).

Currently, versions are available for S-PLUS 2000 for Windows, 5.x and
3.x. Also for R 1.0.

The code can be obtained from

predict.glm.

David ("MathSoft") Smith said "it looks like a bug..[and] it appears to be

warning. This is the approach I'm going to take when those warning messages
prove to be too much of an annoyance. Second, he pointed me to

a page maintained by Thomas Yee which contains Yee and Hastie's "smart
prediction" code. This set of functions (with both S-PLUS and R versions)
takes care of predicting with data-dependent transformations, like x -
min(x), or with splines and other stuff. Thanks for the tip!

Finally, Gerard ("All Others Bring Data") Jean noted an additional problem
with predict.glm(); it chokes when a data frame has had a new level added to
some factor variable, even if no observation takes on that level. Again
predict.gam() can handle this.

messages.subject_clean: Specifying position of minor tick marks for trellis
messages.body_plain:
In S-Plus 6.0 (and perhaps earlier) there is a powerful 
date-time variable class called
timeDate.  Through the scales=list(x=...) option to xyplot 
it is possible to plot date-time variables fairly easily

nTimeDate <- function(x, ...) {
  if(!inherits(x,'timeDate')) stop('x is not a timeDate variable')
  u <- axis.time(range(x,na.rm=T),
                 skip.weekends=F, ...)$grid
  at <- list(at=as.numeric(u$major.grid$x),
             labels=format(u$major.grid$x))
  # minor tick locations: u$minor$x
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  attr(x,'scale') <- at
  x
}

x <- nTimeDate(mytimeDatevar)   # convert to ordinary numeric
xyplot(y ~ x, scales=list(x=attr(x,'scale')))

scales= will label the x-axis nicely, using the fairly well-chosen
time intervals selected by axis.time.  axis.time also computes
positions for minor tick marks (see comment above).
These may be aligned to quarters, months, or weeks.  How would
one specify the minor tick x-axis locations to trellis?
I don't want to use a low-level routine such as axis( ) as
multiple panels may be present.

messages.subject: scan(): could not skip lines
messages.body_plain:
Splus 5.1 on Solaris.

I have a "process monitoring" type of task.

Data is being added to a file by an external non-Splus process, one 
record per minute.

My Splus script uses scan() to read the data into an Splus object, 
notes how many records were read, and periodically updates itself, 
using the skip argument of scan to get only the new records. 
"Periodically" means, say, once every 5 minutes. Eventually, the 
script will run in batch mode as a unix cron job.

Every once in a while, I get an error message like this:

Reading data from  rm_3.dat

Skipping first 5111 lines

Problem in scanDefault(file, what, n, sep = ",", skip = ..2): Could 
not skip 5111 lines in file

If I immediately restart the Splus script, it successfully reads the 
file,skipping the appropriate number of records.

I suspect what is happening is that occasionally Splus tries to read 
the file while it is being written to by the other process. I don't 
know how to test or confirm this suspicion.

Can anyone confirm my suspicion, or suggest a way to test my idea, or 
point me in the correct direction if I'm wrong?

My next step in solving this myself is to experiment with taking more 
control over the file opening and reading process, particularly the 
'blocking' option to the file() and open() functions. Which leads to 
another question:

Does scan() used by itself in Splus 5.1 use the 'new' i/o system, 
e.g., the connection class, or does it use some older method? If it 
uses the new method, does it set blocking=T or blocking=F?

Chapter 10, Section 10.5.3, of Programming with Data has a discussion 
of blocking and non-blocking connections and how to use them and why 
that I don't fully understand yet. (and, did MathSoft fully implement 
this aspect of S?)

Thanks
-Don

We have for some time used Sun hardware for our departmental servers, most

messages.subject: Re: Repeating a function
messages.body_plain:
Two possibilities.  If your function can be vectorized to run on multiple
arguments at once, that's the way to go.  If not, you can use a loop.

Define a vector (or matrix, or array, if the output
of your function is multidimensional) to hold the repeats, then fill it:

results <- numeric(n)
for(i in 1:n) results[n] <- function(args)
mean(results)

The loop can also be built into your function, if you're going to do this
frequently.  Presumably function() generates some random numbers or is
taking different arguments each time, so it doesn't give the same answer
each time. 

If you've got a matrix or array of results, you can use apply to average
over the correct dimensions.

Hope this helps,

Matt

messages.subject: Re: multivariate K function/L function
messages.body_plain:
Janine Illian writes:

> I am using SPLUS 2000 and would like to analyse some marked point pattern
> data (qualitative marks).
> Have any of you ever used SPLUS to calculate the multivariate K-function/
> L-function in this context?

Yes; this is implemented in `spatstat',
available from
        http://www.maths.uwa.edu.au/~adrian/spatstat.html

Here's a typical worked example. 
The text file "mydata" contains data in table format
with each row containing entries x, y, m representing the (x,y) coordinates
of a point and its mark value m. The window of observation is (say)
the rectangle [0,10] x [0, 5].

        df <- read.table("mydata", header=T)
        df$marks <- factor(df$marks, levels=c("Cold", "Warm", "Hot"))

        pp <- point.pattern(df$x, df$y, c(0,10), c(0,5), marks=df$m)

        plot(pp)

        # univariate K-function
        K <- Kest(pp)
        plot(K$r, K$border, type="l", xlab="r", ylab="K(r)")
        lines(K$r, pi * K$r^2, lty=2)

        # cross K-function
        Khc <- Kcross(pp, "Hot", "Cold")        
        plot(Khc$r, Khc$border, type="l", xlab="r", ylab="Kcross(r)")
        lines(Khc$r, pi * Khc$r^2, lty=2)

The plots can be done more elegantly using plot.formula():
        plot(border ~ r, data=Khc)

The L-function is done by hand:
        plot(sqrt(border/pi) ~ r, data=Khc)

====
Prof Adrian Baddeley, Mathematics & Statistics, University of Western Australia
                <http://maths.uwa.edu.au/~adrian/>

In response to my query (below) I received three answers. Thanks very
kindly to those who responded.

I asked:
I am performing a spectral analysis of a temperature series (> ten
thousand records), but I have a few hundred scattered missing values. I
also know that the missing values are averages of adjacent values.
1. How does spec.pgram deal with missing values? I was thinking I might
interpolate the missing values in order to run spec.pgram. How? I was
thinking about checking each record one at a time with an if statement
inside a for statement, but didn't like where that was headed.
2. Also, I would like to test whether the series differs from random
white noise. Any suggestions?

Simon Rosenfeld wrote:
In my view, simple schemes like linear interpolation substantially distort
reality because of multi-spectral nature of temperature variations. Here is
a brief outline of the scheme I
finally ended up with. It is  a four-steps procedure.
1. Extract trends and periodic variations. This step does not require all
the data, missings are OK.
2. Compute variance of detrended data and generate random gaussian noise
with this variance. Fill your gaps (NAs) with this noise.
3. Compute autocorrelation function (this step requires all the data
points,
NAs are not acceptable)
4. OPTIMALLY  interpolate your data using ACF into your gaps

This method is satisfactory until you don't try to study probabilistic
properties of your series. Spectral properties
are preserved in most cases if number of your gaps is reasonably small (up
to 15% of all data) and if they themselves do not
follow a certain spectral pattern (for example, missings are more frequent
in winter than in summer, etc)

If you want a more careful analysis and want to preserve also the
probabilistic structure (for substantially non-gaussian series)
you need couple more steps with non-linear transformations

Matthew Zack wrote:
With respect to your second question, two statistical tests have been used
to test for white noise in spectral analysis:  Fisher's kappa statistic and

Bartlett's Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (Fuller WA.  Introduction to statistical

time series.  New York:  John Wiley & Sons, Inc., 1976).

If you define the amplitude periodogram, J(k), as

   J(k) = 0.5*n*(a(k)**2 + b(k)**2)

     where n=the number of observations in the time series,
           a(k)=the cosine coefficient at k
           b(k)=the sine coefficients at k

then Fisher's kappa statistic tests whether the largest, J(k), differs
statistically significantly from the mean of the J(k).

Bartlett's Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares the normalized cumulative
periodogram,
F(j), of the series

   F(j) = [sum of (k=1 to k=j of J(k)] / [sum of (k=1 to k=m of J(k)],

      where m=n/2 if n is even, (n-1)/2 if n is odd, and j=1,2,3,. . .m-1.

to the cumulative distribution function of a uniform(0,1) random variable
using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. I don't know whether an S-PLUS
implementation of these tests is available.

messages.subject: lm question
messages.body_plain:
The following is a simple example to illustrating a bizarre feature I
noticed.

The problem relates to the multiple r-squared value obtained using lm.

The following creates two vectors, x and y. 

> x_seq(1,10,length=100)
> y_2+x*4+rnorm(100,0,4)
> plot(x,y)

Now perform two fits:

> fit.a_lm(y~x)
> fit.c_lm(y~rep(1,100)+x-1)

As you can see fit.a and fit.c are the same fit. fit.c says fit without an
intercept but fit with a vector of 1's.  As one would expect, the
coefficients from the two models are the same:

> coef(fit.a)
 (Intercept)        x 
    1.512145 4.173989

> coef(fit.c)
 rep(1, 100)        x 
    1.512145 4.173989

The R^2 values, however, are not the same.

> summary(fit.a)$r.squared
[1] 0.8680936
> summary(fit.c)$r.squared 
[1] 0.9752623

It seems as if the R^2 value from fit.a is correct:

> cor(fitted(fit.a),y)^2
[1] 0.8680936
> cor(fitted(fit.c),y)^2
[1] 0.8680936

Any explanations as to the different behavior?

Thanks.
Jason

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The following version of acf (acf.n - with a quick fix - ) tested only 
on S-plus 5.1 (Unix version) will add a title desired. 

e.g acf.n(rnorm(20), main = "test") generates the plot with test as title.

"acf.n" <- 
function(x, lag.max, type = "correlation", plot = T, main = NULL)
{
        ## Handle new and old style time series differently
        if(is(x, "series")) {
                isNewStyle <- T
                xOrig <- x
                xunit <- NULL
                freq <- 1
                x <- seriesData(x)
        }
        else {
                isNewStyle <- F
                x <- as.rts(x)
                tspx <- tspar(x)
                freq <- frequency(x)
                xunit <- units(x)
        }
        if(is.factor(x) || (is.data.frame(x) && any(sapply(x, "is.factor"))))
                stop("Cannot calculate the acf of factors")
        if(is.cts(x))
                freq <- 1
        if(is.data.frame(x))
                x <- numerical.matrix(x)
        else if(!is.matrix(x))
                x <- as.matrix(x)
        n <- dim(x)[1]
        nser <- dim(x)[2]
        dnames <- dimnames(x)[[2]]
        correlation <- partial <- FALSE
        itype <- charmatch(type, c("covariance", "correlation", "partial"),
                nomatch = 0)
        switch(itype + 1,
                stop("desired type of ACF is unknown"),
                {
                        correlation <- FALSE
                        type <- "covariance"
                }
                ,
                {
                        correlation <- TRUE
                        type <- "correlation"
                }
                ,
                {
                        partial <- TRUE
                        type <- "partial"
                }
                )
        x <- scale(x, T, F)
        storage.mode(x) <- "single"
        ier <- .Fortran("tsmiss",
                NAOK = T,
                x,
                as.integer(n),
                as.integer(nser),
                integer(1),
                integer(1),
                as.integer(0),
                specialsok = T)
        if(ier[[6]] > 0)
                stop("There are missing values in midst of time series")
        lo <- ier[[4]]
        ngood <- ier[[5]]
        x <- x[lo:(lo + ngood - 1),  ]
        if(missing(lag.max))
                lag.max <- as.integer(10 * log10(ngood/nser))
        else lag.max <- as.integer(lag.max)
        # make lag.max an integer
        if(lag.max <= 0) stop("lag.max must be positive")
        if(lag.max > ngood) {
                lag.max <- ngood - 1
                warning("lag.max > series length : reduced to series length - 1"
                        )
        }
        r <- array(0, dim = c(lag.max + 1, nser, nser))
        lag <- r
        storage.mode(r) <- "single"
        mlag <- .Fortran("mlag",
                as.integer(ngood),
                as.integer(ngood),
                as.integer(nser),
                as.integer(lag.max),
                x,
                single(nser),
                r = r)
        r <- mlag$r
        if(!partial)
                acf <- (.Fortran("mlag1",
                        as.integer(ngood),
                        as.integer(nser),
                        as.integer(lag.max),
                        r = r,
                        as.logical(correlation)))[[4]]
        else {
                a <- array(0, dim = c(nser, nser, lag.max))
                storage.mode(a) <- "single"
                partialacf <- a
                den <- array(0, dim = c(nser, nser))
                storage.mode(den) <- "single"
                acf <- .Fortran("ar",
                        as.integer(ngood),
                        as.integer(nser),
                        as.integer(lag.max),
                        r,
                        integer(1),
                        den,
                        a,
                        single(lag.max + 1),
                        single(lag.max + 1),
                        a,
                        a,
                        den,
                        den,
                        den,
                        den,
                        partialacf = partialacf,
                        ier = as.integer(0))
                if(acf$ier != 0)
                        stop("cannot invert matrix")
                acf <- aperm(acf$partialacf, c(3, 1, 2))
        }
        lag[1:(lag.max + 1),  ,  ] <- (0:lag.max)/freq
        for(i in 1:nser) {
                if(nser == i)
                        break
                for(j in (i + 1):nser) {
                        lag[, i, j] <- (0:lag.max)/freq
                        lag[, j, i] <-  - (0:lag.max)/freq
                }
        }
        if(partial)
                lag <- array(lag[-1,  ,  ], dim = c(lag.max, nser, nser))
        series.name <- deparse(substitute(x))
        z <- list(acf = acf, lag = lag, n.used = ngood, type = type, series = 
                series.name, units = xunit)
        if(!is.null(dnames))
                z$snames <- dnames
        if(plot) {
                acf.plot(z, if(nser <= 5) c(nser, nser) else c(5, 5), conf.int
                         = correlation || partial, main = main)
        }
        z
}

messages.subject: formula conversion
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-colleagues:
Many thanks to s+ wizards Bert Gunter 
and Samuel Buttrey for help with my request
on "formula conversion". Combining their ideas I managed to solve 
my problem.

Here is the original posting
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Suppose that I have an expession:
y<-2+x+ a*sin(x)+b*exp(x)+c*x^1.3
I need to create a formula
y~x+sin(x)+exp(x)+x^1.3

And vice versa:
I have a formula
y~x+sin(x)+exp(x)+x^1.3
and coefficients: c0,c1,c2,c3,c4
I need to compute ( I mean to create an expression and evaluate it)
y<-c1+c2*x+ c3*sin(x)+c4*exp(x)+c5*x^1.3

Is that possible to automatically do this kind of conversions in s+?

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Here are the answers (slightly edited)

Here's a way to do the second, as long as it's always an additive model,
so that the separators on the right side are always +'s.

> f <- y~x+sin(x)+exp(x)+x^1.3 # your formula
> x <- 2 # set a value for x
> coefs <- c(1,2,3,4,5) # some coefficients; the first is the constant term

> df <- as.character(f) # puts " ~ " into df[1], "y" into df[2], everything
else into df[3]

> rhs.pieces <- unlist (unpaste (df[3], sep="+")) # separate pieces
> my.expr <- paste (df[2], "<-", coefs[1], "+", paste (coefs[-1], "*",
rhs.pieces, collapse="+")) # put it together...
> eval (parse (text = my.expr))
[1] 49.59556
> 1 + 2 * x + 3 * sin(2) + 4 * exp(2) + 5 * 2^1.3 # check
[1] 49.59556

Okay. The first is a little trickier, but again unpaste (twice) can do the
trick, again assuming there are only *'s and +'s.

f <- expression (y<-2+x+ a*sin(x)+b*exp(x)+c*x^1.3) # starting point
f <- as.character(f) # convert to character

less.than <- (1:nchar(f))[substring (f, 1:nchar(f), 1:nchar(f)) == "<"]
lhs <- substring (f, 1, less.than - 2)                # extract lhs; skip
space and "<"
rhs <- substring (f, less.than + 2, nchar(f)) # extract rhs: skip hyphen and
space

rhs.pieces <- unlist (unpaste (rhs, sep="+"))[-1] # break up, discard
constant
#
# Omit the first piece, which has no "*" in it. To each of the remaining
pieces, apply the unpaste function. The
# result is a matrix from which we want the second row.
#
rhs.pieces[-1] <- unlist (sapply (rhs.pieces[-1], unpaste, sep="*")[2,])
new.expr <- parse (text = paste (lhs, "~", paste (rhs.pieces,
collapse="+")))

Sam Buttrey

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
These tasks are fairly easy using unpaste() 
 
  > z_"5+4x+9x^2"
  > terms<-unpaste(z, sep="+")
  > terms
  [[1]]:
  [1] "5"

  [[2]]:
  [1] "4x"

  [[3]]:
  [1] "9x^2"

  Now you can use lapply to remove the first character from each component
  with substring():

  > terms_lapply(terms, function(x)substring(x,2))
  > terms
  [[1]]:
  [1] ""

  [[2]]:
  [1] "x"

  [[3]]:
  [1] "x^2"

  You can now unlist() this into a vector and use paste on the NONconstant
  terms to rebuild the formula -- you paste the constant term on afterwards.

  > cf_c(3,5)
  > paste(cf,unlist(terms)[-1],sep="*",collapse='+')
  [1] "3*x+5*x^2"    

  Bert

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Thanks again
Albert Horwath

> 
> Can someone tell me why this should be the case, and if I can actually
> test for an interaction between two predictors with these models (using
> anova function)?  

The formula notation is confusing you (and `multivariate' is confusing me,
as this is like multiple linear regression, not multivariate linear
regression: seems the person who wrote that S-PLUS manual made this up as
it is not in the White Book, that I can see).
  
Loess fits a smooth curve or surface in all the input variables. It does
not fit an additive model (a sum of smooth functions of individual
inputs), but gam can.
  
`Interactions' of continuous variables like this make little sense,
but in a linear model they stand for cross-product terms, so
  
y ~ (x + z)^2
  
expands to
  
y ~ x + z + x:z        
  
which is

y = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z + b_3 xz                   

and b_3 xz is the `interaction' x:z in the model.  This is not usually
what you want!

For a gam, you can contrast

gam(y ~ lo(x) + lo(z))
gam(y ~ lo(x, z))

and even do an anova on the pair of models.  However, as they are not
nested, that will make little sense.

I would like to express my gratitude for those who answered and tried
to help my original question about plotting error bars within
Trellis.
Thanks to Marcel Baumgartner, Nick Ellis, Jean Adams, Steve Wofsy,
Patrick Connolly, Henrik Nielsen, Jim Pratt, Madeline Bauer, Frank
Harrel, Martin Maerchler, and John Maindonald.

 - Original question:

Dear S-users:

I would like to plot in my graph both error bars (here the sample
standard deviation of the data or an estimate of the standard
deviation, e.g. the standard error) from X's and Y's. How would a
command-line script for this task look like?
Thanks for your attention and consideration.

 - from Nick Ellis

x<-y<-1:10
plot(x,y)
errbar(x,y,y+x/10,y-x/10,x+y/20,x-y/10,add=T)

This is the modified function
errbar <-
function(x, y, yplus, yminus, xplus, xminus, cap = 0.015, xlab =
as.character(
        substitute(x)), ylab = as.character(substitute(y)), add = F, lty = 1,
        ylim, lwd = 1, ...)
{
        if(missing(ylim))
                ylim <- range(y, yplus, yminus, na.rm = T)
        if(!add)
                plot(x, y, ylim = ylim, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, ...)
        xcoord <- par()$usr[1:2]
        segments(x, yminus, x, yplus, lty = lty, lwd = lwd)
        smidge <- (cap * (xcoord[2] - xcoord[1]))/2
        segments(x - smidge, yminus, x + smidge, yminus, lwd = lwd)
        segments(x - smidge, yplus, x + smidge, yplus, lwd = lwd)
        if(!missing(xplus)) {
                segments(xminus, y, xplus, y, lty = lty, lwd = lwd)
                ycoord <- par()$usr[3:4]
                smidge <- (cap * (ycoord[2] - ycoord[1]))/2
                segments(xminus, y - smidge, xminus, y + smidge, lwd = lwd)
                segments(xplus, y - smidge, xplus, y + smidge, lwd = lwd)
        }
}

 - from Jean Adams

x <- sample(5, 100, T)
y <- rnorm(100)
uniq.x <- sort(unique(x))
mean.y <- tapply(y, x, mean)
sd.y <- sqrt(tapply(y, x, var))
error.bar(uniq.x, mean.y, sd.y)

errorbar<-function(x, y, plusmin, size = 0.2)
{
        plot(x, y, ylim = c(min(y - plusmin), max(y + 
                plusmin)), type = "b")
        segments(x, y + plusmin, x, y - plusmin)
        par.cin.x <- par()$cin[1]
        segments(x - size * par.cin.x, y - plusmin, x + 
                size * par.cin.x, y - plusmin)
        segments(x - size * par.cin.x, y + plusmin, x + 
                size * par.cin.x, y + plusmin)
}
